# Time Continuity

- Write a Cut description as **what is visible at the instant that Cut begins** — not how it looks after the action has finished. The still is that Cut's first frame, so if the still for 'turns their head and looks at the sea' already shows the head fully turned, the clip has no action left and stands still for the whole 3–8 seconds.
- When you want a climax standing as a picture, do not write the climax into that Cut's description — **split the Cut and make the climax the first instant of the next one**. That is how film emphasises in the first place.
- A large prop that drives the event (a helicopter, a car, equipment) needs **its state at that instant written into every Cut from the one it enters to the one it leaves** — airborne just before landing, then settled with the rotors still turning, then rotors stopped. Miss it in one Cut and it disappears from that Cut entirely. Writing only the effect is also missing it: 'the wind the helicopter threw up' becomes a person shielding their forehead for no reason on an empty deck with no helicopter.
- A beat where two people touch (a handshake, an offered hand, a grip) needs **the distance and the touch between them** written down. Leave it out and 'does not take the offered hand' is drawn as two people several steps apart, each facing the camera.
- Nail whatever this work has to hold — the helmet under an arm, which side the scar is on, the letters on a name tag — into the **first sentence** of the description. Inside one Draft, the Scenes whose action and props were pinned into the text Cut by Cut (an arm across the way, then the helmet held, then the hand on the lever) ran visibly better, and only the Scenes whose text did not pin the world fell apart.
- **Know the three things that carry over on their own.** The still pass reads every Cut in the Scene at once, so each Cut also receives the world at its own first instant. The clip pass carries, beside the camera movement, the motion the Cut description names, and adds the next Cut's first instant in the same Scene as the arrival point (a Scene's last Cut settles and closes). None of the three is stored; they are built just before generation, so fixing the text means the next generation receives the new sentence.
- **animaticPrompt is filled in while the Storyboard bakes.** In a Scene with more than one Cut, one line of motion lands in that field for each Cut — it comes out of the same reading as the three above, so it cannot contradict the sentence the still receives. Unlike the three, this one stays in the field, so it can be read and corrected on screen after the bake.
- **So your job is not to fill it in but to read it back after the bake.** Bake the Scene, skim those fields, and use update_cuts to correct only the lines whose direction is wrong or that let people, costume, props, or background in. Start with the Cuts whose first frame is a held pose (a body afloat, an outstretched hand) — those are the ones where a flipped direction turns a sinking Scene into a rising video. Do not fill 124 Cuts in by hand from scratch.
- **A Scene with only one Cut is left blank** — there is no neighbour to join to, so that Scene never runs this reading at all. Its clip carries the Cut description instead, so fill it in by hand whenever the direction matters for that Cut.
- Fill it in and it is carried **instead of** the description — the two are never carried together. The camera movement and the arrival point stay either way.
- When filling it in, **write motion only — leave out people, costume, props, and background.** The first frame is the finished picture itself, so those pixels already hold them, and writing them again buries the direction under that description. Measured on the same Cut and the same first frame with only the prompt changed: the wetsuit stayed without one word about clothing, and only the version that wrote clothing and surroundings put a large object across the foreground.
- **Name what moves the opposite way alongside it** — 'the body toward the lower edge, the droplets toward the upper'. That one pair is what fixed the direction.
- **Do not write the camera** — clipCameraMovement is carried separately, so two directions fight.
- **Vertical motion cannot come from the camera — design it from the subject and its surroundings.** Put Crane Up or Crane Down in clipCameraMovement and this video model produces a Dolly (a push in which background and subject grow in proportion). Five runs on the same Cut and the same first frame did it five times out of five, and a rule-abiding prompt did not save it either. Tilt is no substitute — only one of two runs carried a vertical axis at all, and neither carried the intended direction (a body written to sink rose instead). For a sinking Cut, do not try to lower the camera: write the pair above ('the body toward the lower edge, the droplets toward the upper') into animaticPrompt. It saves, but one warning comes with it — not because the value was removed from the advertised options, but because what lost is the video model currently attached rather than the value, so it is a place to measure again when the model changes.
- **A camera moving closer cannot come out either — carry the weight with something small on screen, or with Cut length.** Put Dolly In in clipCameraMovement and this video model produces a still frame. Shortening the movement sentence, halving the pacing, dropping the last line — all four runs did it, so this is not a place a prompt can save. **Dolly Out, moving away, came out in all four runs.** When the Cut description already has a body in motion (reaching out a hand, a chair turning), leave the movement Static — that action fills the screen. The camera sentence that does not come out was only competing with it.
- **Do not invent a body a still face or object never had.** A name-tag insert, a console screen, a listening face — when the subject moves closer there, the direction breaks: a name tag cannot come toward the camera, and a listener who suddenly leans in loses whatever that Cut was for. What such a Cut wanted from Dolly In was not the approach but the weight of 'look at this'. Carry that weight by writing **something small** on screen into animaticPrompt (an eye blinks once, a line of screen text scrolls, light travels across a metal surface), or by accepting it as a still Cut and giving **Cut length** the upper end of that beat's range. The three above (Dolly In, Crane, Tilt) were not removed from the advertised options — **they are a place to measure again when the model changes**: a different video model was the exact opposite, Dolly In in all four runs and Dolly Out in only one of four.
- **Leaving the clip field blank does not get you out of it.** When the clip movement is blank the video uses the Storyboard field's cameraMovement instead, so if that field says Crane the same value goes out. The video doors (animate_cut, animate_draft) measure not what is written in a field but **the movement this clip will actually go out with**, and raise one warning then (one per Cut, one even when both fields say Crane). The still doors (generate_storyboard, finalize_render) stay quiet — the measurements came from video only, and nobody has yet measured what Crane draws on a still.
- These three fields (animaticPrompt, clipCameraMovement, clipEasing) **can go in with add_scene and add_cut when the Cut is created.** If you already know while splitting Cuts that 'this Cut sinks', write it then — **a hand-written value is never overwritten by the pipeline.** Come back with update_cuts after everything is baked, finalised, and filmed, and it produces those video values again.
- A Cut's first instant is attached **only when the Scene has two or more Cuts**. Redraw a single Cut with regenerate_cut and there is no neighbour to join to, so that Cut is drawn without it — when the redraw is meant to fix a boundary, give regenerate_board that Scene's id instead.
- One honest limit: this joining **only meshes when the place the clip heads toward and the place the next Cut's still drew are the same**. In a Draft whose stills were baked before these features, the clip goes to a place the still never drew — there the hand prescription (the world at that instant in the description's first sentence) still holds, and the root fix is re-baking that Scene's stills.
- One more: **a boundary that jumps several shot sizes** (Full → Close-Up) is not caught automatically. The next Cut's first instant is a sentence true only in the next Cut's frame, so a frame three steps away receives it and the two disagree. Look at those boundaries yourself.
- Once a Scene's clips are all out, look at that Scene's Cuts together with review_clips — it names the first frame and the last frame separately. Ask about whatever this work must hold with asks, one line per Cut (the letters on a name tag, which side the scar is on, the helmet). The paid scale and the skipping are in animatics.md.
- When a boundary is in doubt, put **the previous clip's last moment** and **the next clip's first instant** side by side and ask whether it is the same world — is the prop that was there before still there, how many people and where, is the costume the same.
- **Fix a diverged boundary in the text before re-baking** — nail the world at that instant into the first sentence of the later Cut's description, and write where that prop is into the earlier Cut's. Re-baking with no information upstream is a lottery, and a paid one.
- **Rule Check does not look at this axis — deliberately.** Whether a prop disappeared can only be judged by knowing what it means, which cannot be made precise as a single rule, and a half-made warning kills the whole rulebook. Do not read the absence of a warning as the boundaries being sound — what has been looked at is only the Cuts you looked at with review_clips.
- A paid full audit that counts the whole Draft is run by a separate harness on the director's side (`backend/scripts/continuity/boundary_audit.py`). The Assistant Director has no such hand, so say so when the director asks for a full count.

Complete when: Every Cut description in the touched Scene opens at that shot's first instant instead of its finished action, every event prop carries its own state in each Cut from the one it enters to the one it leaves, and every contact beat states the distance and touch between the people. Every animaticPrompt the board pass wrote was read back after the bake, and only the wrong lines were corrected—each surviving line motion alone, no people, costume, props, background, or camera word, and naming what moves the opposite way beside what moves—while a Cut standing alone in its Scene, which that pass skips, was filled by hand whenever its direction mattered. No Cut asks the camera to rise, fall, or move closer: every rise or fall is built from the subject and its surroundings, and every push toward a subject is carried either by motion the Cut description already holds or by the Cut's own length, because this video model turns Crane into a dolly, Tilt into neither axis nor direction, and Dolly In into a still frame. No still insert, screen, or listening face was given a body it did not have in order to replace that push. Every boundary the director doubted was checked by putting one clip's last moment beside the next clip's first through review_clips and was corrected in the Cut text before any paid regeneration, and a Draft whose stills predate this continuity work—or a boundary that jumps several shot sizes—was named as needing eyes rather than reported as covered.
